title: Pro Risk Management
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/0/body: Once the price has moved far enough your way (say **1R**), you move your stop loss to your **entry price**. From then on, the worst case is roughly **breakeven** (minus costs and slippage).
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/1/body: A **trailing stop** is a stop loss that **follows the price** as it moves your way, but never moves back. You can trail it at a fixed distance (say 30 pips), a multiple of ATR, or below **each new higher low (HL)**.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/1/visual/symbol: Stop below the latest higher low
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: You bought Ethereum at $3,000 with a stop loss at $2,900. Your rule: when the price moves 1R your way, go risk-free. When, and where do you move the stop?
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/2/explanation: Risk (1R) = 3,000 − 2,900 = $100, so +1R is 3,100. Going risk-free means moving the stop to your entry price, 3,000. Moving the stop further back (2,800) is the opposite of what you want.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: You bought EUR/USD at 1.0800 with a 40-pip trailing stop. The price rose to 1.0900 and then turned back. Where does the trade close, and what's the result?
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/3/explanation: The stop always stays 40 pips below the highest price: 1.0900 − 0.0040 = 1.0860. Exiting there locks in 60 pips of profit.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/4/prompt: You bought in this uptrend and move your stop loss below each new higher low (HL). Tap the candle whose low your stop should now sit under.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/4/explanation: This is the latest higher low: after it, the price rallied and made a new high. The earlier lows are lower, and a stop loss never moves back.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/5/statement: In a buy trade, when the price drops, you move your trailing stop lower too.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/5/explanation: A trailing stop only moves toward profit. Moving it lower means adding risk, exactly when the market is against you.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/6/prompt: Your buy is in profit, but the stop loss is still under the first higher low. Using the "below the latest HL" rule, drag the stop loss line up to its new spot.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/6/explanation: The latest higher low (HL) formed at 3110, so the stop goes a little below it, say 3100. If the price breaks that low, the uptrend structure is broken. If you stay under the previous HL (3040), you give back more profit for no reason.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/7/body: Going risk-free **too early** can knock you out on a normal pullback, and you miss the main move. Many traders wait until the price has moved at least **1R** or made a new **higher low**, and only then move the stop.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/prompt: Put the management of a buy trade in order.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/items/0: Enter with an initial stop loss
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/items/2: Move the stop loss to your entry price
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/items/3: Raise the stop below each higher low
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/items/4: Exit when the trailing stop gets hit
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/8/explanation: First the risk is limited, then it's removed (risk-free), and then the trailing stop locks in profit step by step.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/9/sentence: Moving the stop loss to your entry price is known as ___, and a stop loss that trails behind the price is called a ___.
lessons/risk-u3-l1/steps/9/explanation: Breakeven brings your risk down to about zero; after that, a trailing stop follows the price and locks in profit.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/0/body: Some assets usually move **together**. For example, EUR/USD and GBP/USD often move the same way, because both are traded against the **dollar**. If you buy both, you've really placed **one big bet** on the dollar weakening.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/1/body: Three 1% trades on **correlated** assets behave almost like **one 3% trade**: if your idea is wrong, all three hit their stop losses together.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/2/prompt: Which combination has the most same-direction risk?
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/2/options/0: Buy EUR/USD, buy GBP/USD and sell USD/CHF
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/2/explanation: All three trades in the first option mean "the dollar will weaken." In the second option, one bets on dollar weakness and one on dollar strength, so they partly cancel each other out.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/3/statement: Buying EUR/USD while selling USD/CHF counts as a kind of diversification.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/3/explanation: Both mean "the dollar will weaken." These two pairs usually have a strong negative correlation, so buying one and selling the other piles your risk onto one idea instead of spreading it.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/4/prompt: You have buy positions on Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and one other altcoin, each at 1.5% risk. If the whole crypto market dumps, roughly what's your real risk?
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/4/explanation: In big sell-offs, most altcoins fall along with Bitcoin. So 4 × 1.5% = about 6% risked on one idea: "crypto goes up."
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/5/body: **Total risk** is the sum of the risk on all your open trades: how much you'd lose if every stop loss got hit at once. Many traders cap their total risk (say 5%) and set a separate cap for each correlated group (say 2%).
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/6/prompt: Your account is $20,000 and you have three open trades risking $200, $200 and $300. What's your total portfolio risk?
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/6/explanation: 200 + 200 + 300 = $700, and 700 ÷ 20,000 = 3.5%. That's how much you'd lose if every stop loss got hit at once.
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/7/pairs/0/meani: Usually move in the same direction
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/7/pairs/2/meani: The sum of risk on all open trades
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/8/prompt: You have a EUR/USD buy open at 1% risk, and now you spot a GBP/USD buy setup. Your rule: max 1.5% risk on one idea. What's the most sensible move?
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/8/options/0: Enter at 0.5% risk so the idea stays at 1.5%
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/8/options/2: Enter at 2% risk because the setup is stronger
lessons/risk-u3-l2/steps/8/explanation: Both trades bet on a "weak dollar." At 0.5%, the total risk on this idea stays at 1.5%, and your rule holds.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/0/body: Even with a **positive expectancy**, if your risk per trade is too high, you can go **broke** before your edge has a chance to show. The chance of reaching the point where you can't keep going is called **risk of ruin**.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/1/body: A system with a 50% win rate and a 1:1.5 ratio has an expectancy of **+0.25R**. Now look at a 10-loss streak (which will happen sooner or later) at two risk levels:
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/2/prompt: Your system's win rate is 45%; each win averages 2R and each loss 1R. What's the expectancy?
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/2/explanation: (0.45 × 2) − (0.55 × 1) = 0.9 − 0.55 = +0.35R. With $100 of risk, each trade is worth about $35 on average.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/3/statement: When your system has a positive expectancy, your risk per trade doesn't matter.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/3/explanation: Expectancy is only the long-run average. With high risk, a normal losing streak can wipe out your account before you ever reach the long run.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/prompt: With a 40% win rate, the chance of seeing at least one streak of 10 losses in a row within 500 trades is about 70%. Which conclusion is right?
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/options/0: Set your risk so that 10 losses in a row are survivable
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/options/1: That's practically impossible, so don't worry about it
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/options/2: After 5 losses, double your size to win it back
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/options/3: You can never make money with a 40% win rate
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/4/explanation: Over lots of trades, a long losing streak is almost certain. At 1% risk, 10 losses cause about a 10% drawdown; at 5%, about 40%. And a 40% win rate can be profitable with a good reward.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/5/body: Here are the priorities: first **staying alive** (low risk per trade and a cap on total risk), then a **positive edge**, then **growth**. Risking around **0.5 to 2%** per trade keeps normal losing streaks survivable.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/5/tip: The market always offers new opportunities; an account at zero doesn't.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/prompt: Two traders use the same system (expectancy +0.3R). The first risks 1% per trade and the second 10%. Who's more likely to still be trading five years from now?
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/options/0: The first, because a losing streak won't wipe them out
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/options/1: The second, because they build profit faster
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/options/2: No difference, since their system is the same
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/options/3: The second, because more risk is always better
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/6/explanation: Same system, different fates: at 10% risk, a 10-loss streak takes about 65% of the account. The first trader stays in long enough for the edge to work.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/7/sentence: A positive expectancy is necessary, but it isn't ___; without low risk, you could be ___ before it pays off.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/7/explanation: A positive edge only shows up over lots of trades; risk management makes sure you're still in the game by then.
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/0/meani: The average value of each trade
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/1/meani: The chance of losing the ability to go on
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/9/prompt: Put it all together. What's this trader's biggest danger?
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/9/options/0: A normal losing streak could wipe out the account
lessons/risk-u3-l3/steps/9/explanation: Three correlated trades at 8% means about 24% risk on one idea. And 10 losses in a row at 8% take about 57% of the account. A positive edge won't save this trader.
